# F02 — Compensated demand and price changes

Original synthetic lecture material, version 1. Continues F01.

## Slide 1 — A different optimization question

Ordinary demand holds income fixed and maximizes utility. Hicksian demand holds a positive target utility ubar fixed and minimizes expenditure. Explain which variables are inputs and which are outcomes. In this xy model the target is attained at equality.

## Slide 2 — Derivation

Write E(x)=px*x+py*ubar/x for x>0. Derive hx=sqrt(py*ubar/px), hy=sqrt(px*ubar/py) and expenditure e=2*sqrt(px*py*ubar). Check minimum and the positive-root choice. Show why hy/hx=px/py and explain it using tangency, not just algebra.

## Slide 3 — Finite Hicks decomposition, worked example

u=xy, M=32, initial px=py=1, new px=4, py=1. Define A as old actual optimum, B as new-price/old-utility compensated optimum, C as new actual optimum at original income. Find both coordinates, utility and expenditure at all three points. Compute the x substitution effect B-A and income effect C-B, and verify their sum. Why can B cost more than actual income although nominal income has not changed in the real experiment?

## Slide 4 — Geometry

Draw x horizontally and y vertically. Show the old budget line, new actual budget line, and parallel compensated line tangent to the old indifference curve. Label A, B, C consistently with slide 3; explain which two points share utility and which two price ratio. Show how the interpretation identifies the effects even when point labels are changed.

## Slide 5 — A distinct compensation

Compare the income needed at new prices to buy the old bundle with the minimum income needed to attain old utility. Compute both for slide 3. The former is a purchasing-power compensation associated with the finite Slutsky construction; it is not the Hicks middle bundle. Explain why the two compensations need not be equal. No differential Slutsky equation is required in this miniature course.

## Slide 6 — Direction and assumptions

For the xy model both goods are normal because ordinary demands increase with income at fixed prices. Do not infer that an income effect must always have this direction for every preference or every good. Relate the two negative x effects in slide 3 to the actual assumptions.
